task: Our Go binary runs as PID 1 inside a container (its own PID namespace). When it gets SIGTERM and has no signal handler installed, it exits with status 2 instead of looking like it was killed by the signal. runc users have reported the same thing. Why does this happen, and what does the runtime do about it?
gold: The kernel does not terminate PID 1 on a default-action fatal signal (SIGTERM etc. with no handler), so the runtime's dieFromSignal, which assumes the kernel will kill the process, falls through to its last-resort exit(2)
The fix (runtime/signal_unix.go dieFromSignal) replaces exit(2) with exit(128+sig), mimicking the shell convention for a child terminated by a signal

Installing custom SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers is a workaround but was not acceptable for runc because it needs an extra goroutine; an earlier idea of doing nothing for PID 1 was dropped as a possible breaking change

task: A test inside a testing/synctest bubble hangs forever as soon as it calls timer.Reset(0) on a time.Timer. The same code outside synctest is fine. What is going on?
gold: Since Go 1.23 timer channels are synchronous, and runtime.timer.modify locks the timer's sendLock mutex for a (non-async) channel timer
With a 0 duration the bubbled timer is run immediately via unlockAndRun, which locks the same sendLock again, so the mutex is locked twice and it deadlocks
The fix in runtime/time.go unlocks the held sendLock before running the bubbled timer immediately (issue #76052)

task: With http.Transport.MaxConnsPerHost set, after some requests are cancelled, later requests to the same host just hang forever waiting for a connection. What causes this?
gold: Transport.dialConnFor has an early return when the wanted connection's dial context is nil (the request was already cancelled/done), skipping the dial
That early-return path did not call decConnsPerHost, so the per-host connection count leaked and later requests blocked on the MaxConnsPerHost limit
Fix: call t.decConnsPerHost(w.key) before returning on that path in net/http/transport.go (issue #65705)

task: A security report says os.Root.Chmod on Linux can change the permissions of a file outside the root if an attacker swaps the target for a symlink at the right moment, even though Root.Chmod checks for symlinks first. How is that possible and how was it fixed?
gold: On Linux the fchmodat syscall silently ignores the AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW flag, so a symlink swapped in after Root.Chmod's check (a TOCTOU race) is followed
The fix makes internal/syscall/unix Fchmodat on Linux use the fchmodat2 syscall (Linux 6.6+) when available
When fchmodat2 is unavailable it uses the glibc/musl workaround: open the target with O_PATH (no follow) and chmod it via /proc/self/fd (CVE-2026-32282, issue #78293)

task: errors.Join always allocates a new joinError. Could we just return the error itself when Join is called with a single error that already implements Unwrap() []error, to save the allocation?
gold: That exact optimization was added (CL 635115) and then reverted
Reason: the new behavior did not match the function's documentation (Join is documented to return a new error wrapping the given errors)
Revert fixed issue #76961; a different design would be needed rather than reapplying it

task: I want database drivers to be able to override how Rows.Scan converts values into destination types. Is there a driver-side hook for this in database/sql, or should we add one?
gold: An API letting drivers override Scan behavior was added (CL 588435, planned for Go 1.26) and then reverted, so there is no such hook
Reason: the API was difficult to use correctly and in many cases could not be used efficiently
The problem is reopened (issue #67546) for more design work rather than reapplying that API

task: To stop httputil.ReverseProxy from racing on the outbound request body, can we wrap the outbound body so that Close is a no-op?
gold: That was tried (CL 722160) and reverted
Making Close a no-op caused second-order issues, and net/http's Request.Body contract says Close must unblock a waiting Read, which a no-op-close reader does not do
It was reverted so a better approach can be implemented (issue #75933; fixes #78973 and #80085)

task: On macOS, os.ReadDir("/dev/fd") used to fail in tests with 'bad file descriptor'. What is the platform quirk and how does os handle it now?
gold: A macOS kernel bug: fstat(N) works but lstat("/dev/fd/N") and fstatat on /dev/fd fail with EBADF when N is a kqueue file descriptor
os now treats EBADF like ENOENT while listing a directory and continues the ReadDir loop, so the kqueue fd is simply omitted from the result (issue #80143)
The error message was also changed to include the entry name (fstatat /dev/fd/3 instead of fstatat /dev/fd)

task: On 32-bit Linux the runtime needs the 64-bit time syscalls. Why doesn't it just try them and fall back when it gets ENOSYS?
gold: ENOSYS fallback breaks on Linux forks: on Android 10 and older the seccomp policy kills the process on the unknown 64-bit time syscall instead of returning ENOSYS (#77621)
Old Synology Linux added vendor syscalls without leaving a gap in the numbering, so the newer syscall number is interpreted as a different vendor syscall (#77930)
So the runtime decides using a uname kernel-version check instead of probing the syscall

task: If I leave http.Transport.MaxIdleConnsPerHost at zero, how many idle keep-alive connections per host does the Transport keep, and where is that decided?
gold: It uses DefaultMaxIdleConnsPerHost, which is 2
Decided in net/http/transport.go: Transport.maxIdleConnsPerHost() returns DefaultMaxIdleConnsPerHost when the field is 0
